title: Public adminModuleCall exposes jackpot payout delegatecall
description: LotteryManager4626.adminModuleCall(bytes) was added as a public helper for queue/execute/cancel admin-module calls, but it does not itself enforce onlyOwner or restrict the callable selector set. The comment assumes the admin module enforces onlyOwner, but not every external admin-module function does: payoutLocalJackpot is external onlyDelegateCall and intentionally lacks onlyOwner because it was previously meant to be reachable only from the main contract's internal _payoutLocalJackpot path after a legitimate lottery win. With the new public arbitrary delegatecall, an attacker can call manager.adminModuleCall(abi.encodeWithSelector(LotteryManager4626AdminModule.payoutLocalJackpot.selector, token, attacker, 10000)). In delegatecall context onlyDelegateCall passes, payoutBps=10000 pays 100% of the available jackpot reserve, and the subsequent gauge payJackpot call is made by the LotteryManager contract address, satisfying the gauge's only-lottery-manager check. This enables unauthorized draining of jackpot ShareOFT reserves for active tokens without winning the lottery or being owner.

title: Auto-keep media enables SSRF and secret exfiltration
description: The new auto-keep feature is enabled by default and schedules Pinata pinning for every newly ingested keepable media attachment in Hermit command rooms. The candidate URL comes from chat attachment metadata and is passed to keepHermitMemeFromMedia, which calls pinRemoteMediaToPinata. That helper validates only the initial scheme with /^https:\/\//, then fetches with redirect: 'follow' and no DNS/IP/private-network allowlist. Because the filename is derived from the attacker-controlled original URL or attachment filename, a URL such as https://attacker.example/a.gif can redirect to http://169.254.169.254/... or another internal endpoint; the non-image response can still pass the media check due to the .gif filename and will be uploaded to Pinata/IPFS and stored in hermit_memes. This can expose internal metadata, service responses, or other backend-only data, and can also be abused to consume outbound bandwidth/Pinata quota.

title: Unrestricted /keep media fetch enables SSRF exfiltration
description: The commit introduces a server-side media pinning path for /keep. A room user can cause the backend to fetch the URL from replyMedia and upload the response body to Pinata, then the bot returns the public IPFS gateway URL. pinRemoteMediaToPinata only checks that the original sourceUrl starts with https://, but uses redirect: 'follow' and never validates the final URL, hostname, resolved IP, or whether a redirect downgraded to http://. It also accepts a caller-provided filenameHint as sufficient evidence of an image, so non-image internal responses can pass the media-type check if the attachment filename ends in .gif/.png/.jpg/.webp. This can be abused as SSRF to internal or metadata endpoints reachable from the Vercel/server environment, with successful responses publicly pinned to IPFS/Pinata. The code also buffers the entire upstream response before applying the 12 MB size limit, which increases DoS/billing impact, but the primary issue is SSRF-assisted data exfiltration.

title: OApp sender can leak the global keeper API key
description: In HTTP sender mode, the new OApp sender is intended to authenticate to a separate Solana lottery message-sending service. However, if SOLANA_LOTTERY_OAPP_SEND_TOKEN is unset, the code uses KPR_API_KEY, and in the frontend path also KEEPR_API_KEY, as the outbound Authorization bearer token. KPR_API_KEY is the same secret used by keeper API routes for machine authentication. As a result, any OApp sender endpoint that is less trusted, compromised, misconfigured, or served over an observable transport receives a bearer token that can authenticate to keeper endpoints, not just perform OApp sends. This widens a narrowly scoped transport integration into disclosure of a high-privilege keeper secret and can allow unauthorized keeper API operations.

title: Dynamic room discovery can let unapproved rooms trigger trades
description: The new runtime room resolver no longer restricts reaction rooms to the previously hardcoded supported set. It derives wallets from ALFACLUB_INVERSE_AKITA_ROOM_WALLETS or from an unverified chat JWT payload, reads every AlfaClub FriendKey holding for those wallets, and appends each held tokenId to the trusted reaction-room list. The bridge then polls every such room, parses ordinary chat text as inverse trade intents, and eventually calls runArenaTrade with the strategy/agent wallet after only checking that the sender has at least one staked key in any configured reaction room. If an attacker can cause the discovery wallet to hold a key for an attacker-controlled room, for example by transferring/airdropping a FriendKey, that room becomes a live execution source without an explicit allowlist or owner approval. The commit also publishes this runtime surface at /api/v1/alfaclub/hermit-runtime without session or cron-secret authentication, leaking runtime rooms, bridge auth health, and recent trade-decision metadata.

title: Self-bundled deploys donate withdrawable EntryPoint deposits
description: The new self-bundle path computes a required prefund from the inflated deploy-session gas limits and maxFeePerGas, then sends that ETH to EntryPoint.depositTo(userOp.sender) before calling handleOps. The sender is the deploy-session Coinbase smart wallet, which is controlled by the authenticated creator/session owner. EntryPoint deposits are credited to the sender account, not to the funder or a paymaster escrow, and can be used for later UserOps or withdrawn by the smart wallet via EntryPoint.withdrawTo. Because the deploy wrapper forces very large gas limits and adds a 10% buffer, successful operations can leave withdrawable surplus in the sender deposit; if handleOps fails after the top-up, the prefund remains credited to the sender as well. An authenticated allowlisted deploy user can repeatedly create/continue sessions and withdraw or spend the leftover deposit, draining DEPLOY_SESSION_SELF_BUNDLE_PRIVATE_KEY/PRIVATE_KEY funds and potentially disabling deployment operations.

title: Untrusted forwarded host used as canonical origin
description: The new getCanonicalOrigin() logic returns the request-derived forwarded origin whenever the hostname is not loopback and does not end in .vercel.app. It does not require the host to match APP_ORIGIN, CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS, known 4626 domains, or even HTTPS. Several deploy-session handlers treat getCanonicalOrigin(req) as a trusted same-origin base URL. In particular, deploy/v2/session/start POSTs to `${origin}/api/deploy/v2/session/create` while forwarding Authorization, X-SIWA-Receipt, and Cookie headers, and deploy-session continue/cancel paths may use `${origin}/api/paymaster` while forwarding X-CV-Deploy-Session credentials. Before this commit, production preferred VERCEL_URL and only considered forwarded hosts in non-production with an allowlist. Under the stated threat model where HTTP headers are attacker-controlled, an authenticated attacker can set X-Forwarded-Host to an external or internal hostname and cause the server to make outbound requests to that host with sensitive headers. The same canonical-origin change is also fed into trusted-origin construction, which can incorrectly add the attacker-selected origin to trusted request origins.

title: Cross-room stake gate allows shared-wallet trade control
description: The updated policy no longer binds authorization to the room where the message was posted, the room owner, or the shared executor room. For any message in a configured reaction room, the code checks the sender's FriendKey stake in the message room first and then in every other configured reaction room. Finding one staked key in any of those rooms returns eligible=true. That eligibility is then used to execute a trade through the shared room-1659 InverseAKITA identity. As a result, a user who can obtain or temporarily stake one key in any configured reaction room can post a market opinion in a watched room and cause the bot to open or trim Hyperliquid positions using the shared executor wallet. The per-sender cooldown does not fully mitigate this because multiple staker addresses can be used, and the resulting trades use configured notional/leverage against the executor account.

title: Paymaster can sponsor irreversible AgentToken ownership transfer
description: This commit extends the paymaster's deployment validation to accept Agent-lane phase-2 code IDs and to derive the lane-specific revenue policy controller. However, the later token-call validation still treats `transferOwnership(address)` as valid for any deploy_phase2/deploy_phase3 token as long as the new owner equals `expectedCreatorCoinPolicyController`. For Agent deployments that variable now resolves to the deterministic `AgentRevenuePolicyController`. Unlike `CreatorCoinPolicyController`, `AgentRevenuePolicyController` only exposes `enforceProjectTaxRecipient()` and has no method to transfer token ownership onward or back. A malicious or compromised deploy-session signer could therefore include an extra `transferOwnership(AgentRevenuePolicyController)` call in an Agent deployment UserOperation and have it pass paymaster policy. If the AgentToken is Ownable, this can permanently lock owner-gated AgentToken administration behind a controller that cannot perform general owner actions, causing loss of administrative control and availability for token configuration.

title: Keeper can move Ajna vault buffer into risky buckets
description: AjnaERC4626Vault.moveFromBuffer is the risk-on path that withdraws assets from the idle buffer and supplies them to an Ajna bucket via AJNA_POOL.addQuoteToken. Before this commit it was restricted to AUTH.swapper through onlyAdapterAuthorized. The commit changed it to onlySwapperOrKeeper, so any address marked as a keeper in AjnaVaultAuth can now choose a bucket index and move buffer liquidity into Ajna lending positions. The only on-chain constraints are the bucket-index range/minimum and the configured buffer ratio; there is no oracle check, approved-bucket list, adapter strategy policy, or management approval on the keeper-chosen bucket. A malicious or compromised keeper can therefore reduce withdrawal liquidity to the minimum buffer and place a large portion of strategy assets into poor/manipulated Ajna buckets, causing withdrawal DoS and potentially material strategy losses. Keepers already remain able to call moveToBuffer, which is the safer de-risking direction; moveFromBuffer should remain restricted to the swapper/adapter or a separate explicitly trusted risk-on role with stronger bucket controls.

title: Weak agent-token checks can bypass deploy access gates
description: This commit adds automatic and query-parameter-selected agent-vault deployments. The client considers a token to be an AgentTokenV4 integration if five multicall reads succeed and `pairToken` is non-null, without checking code hash, factory/registry provenance, non-zero/consistent integration addresses, or a trusted AgentTokenV4 registry. The deploy gate then allows deployment if `isAgentTokenReady` is true, bypassing the previous Zora Creator Coin, coin-age, and paid deploy feature checks. On the API side, the phase-1 `vaultKind` is decoded from user calldata and used to select agent bytecode/module checks, but no corresponding validation proves that `creatorToken` is a real supported agent token. The existing session checks trust `creator()`, `payoutRecipient()`, and `owner()` values returned by the untrusted token: authority can be satisfied by returning the attacker's wallet as creator/owner, while allowlist can be satisfied by returning any allowlisted address as payoutRecipient/owner. This lets an unapproved attacker with a canonical smart wallet deploy an agent vault for a malicious token and consume/pollute protected deployment infrastructure.

title: Staker pilot access can overwrite Arena agent identity
description: In `executeCommand`, any room 1659 user who passes `canPilotInverseAkita` is allowed past the coarse `isHermitOperatorOnlyCommand('/arena')` gate and is then passed into `executeHermitCommand` with `isTrustedOperator: true`. However, `executeHermitCommand` treats all `/arena` subcommands as already authorized and does not add subcommand-level checks around privileged operations such as `identity set default`, `identity clear default`, and `register default`. As a result, a non-operator with the minimum InverseAKITA stake can overwrite or clear the room-default Arena identity mapping, bind arbitrary agent wallets, or trigger ACP agent creation/onboarding using the service runtime credentials. This can redirect subsequent trades/status/deposit flows away from the intended InverseAKITA agent/wallet or disrupt the shared executor.

title: Dust fills can trigger oversized rebalance dip orders
description: For strict-inverse room 1659, any user add/reduce fill is routed directly into handlePairedLegRebalanceFlow and then the loop continues before the normal min-notional, cooldown, hourly/daily cap, buffer-floor, risk-gate, and LLM checks run. Inside the rebalance planner, the triggering fill's position-change percentage is computed as rebalancePct, but that value is only used to size the harvest leg. The dip-add leg is instead sized by resolveDrawdownBasedDipAddUsd/resolveMaxCounterNotionalUsd from the losing silo's account value and drawdown, independent of the triggering fill notional or rebalancePct. As a result, a very small add/reduce fill can trigger an `open` order on the losing leg sized at a percentage of the trading fund, with leverage. With defaults this can be up to 10% of the fund per dip response, and room overrides allow much higher percentages. This bypasses the normal trade throttles and can force the bot/user silo into unwanted leveraged exposure.

title: Settled truth gate trusts client-supplied authority
description: This commit attempts to restrict writes of `settledAt` or `settlementStage="completed"` to the sweep-completion path. However, the authority check is implemented as a comparison against the literal public string `sweep-completion`, and keeper endpoints accept that same value directly from untrusted request JSON. Any caller with access to the keeper API bearer token can POST `settledAtAuthority: "sweep-completion"` to `/api/keeper/mark-settled` or `/api/keeper/control-plane/settle` and mark a vault as completed without the sweep handler having run completion invariants. The authority should be derived server-side only from a verified sweep completion result or from an internal job context, not accepted from an HTTP body.

title: Wallet-first waitlist login trusts spoofable email hints
description: The new waitlist login option switches from email-only to wallet-or-email whenever a local prior-auth marker exists or any `verifiedEmailHint` is present. That hint is not a trusted proof of email ownership: it can come from unverified Privy-linked email data or from sessionStorage. After a wallet-only login, the bootstrap request sends this hint as `email`; the server then falls back to `bootstrapEmailHint` when Privy has no verified email, and later upserts the account with `emailVerified: true`. In the collision path, matching the bootstrap hint is also enough to rebind an email already associated with another Privy user. An attacker can therefore authenticate with their own wallet, supply or retain a chosen waitlist email hint, and have the server bind or rebind that email to the attacker's Privy identity without proving control of the email. This can lead to waitlist/account takeover, unauthorized access to gated account state, and integrity loss for points/referral/profile data.

title: Public Hermit DMs execute as AlfaClub room commands
description: The commit adds a private-DM handler for the Hermit Telegram bot. `TELEGRAM_TO_ALFACLUB_DM_ENABLED` defaults to true and an empty `TELEGRAM_TO_ALFACLUB_DM_USER_IDS` set means all Telegram users are allowed. For any private chat hitting the Hermit webhook, the handler passes slash commands through unchanged and, when a room id is configured, calls `executeDeterministicCommand` with `chatId: alfaclub:<roomId>`. The command executor intentionally treats `alfaclub:*` chat IDs as trusted AlfaClub bridge invocations and skips the `HERMIT_ALLOWED_USERS` gate for Hermit commands. As a result, anyone who can DM the public Hermit bot can run room-context Hermit commands despite not being an AlfaClub room member. Room-context commands include `/position markers all` and `/position marker <n>`, which read and return room timeline data including trade markers and chat text/replies. Media commands such as `/gmeow` can also be treated as AlfaClub-originated and may trigger system X posting when configured. The fix should make DM handling opt-in or require a non-empty allowlist/membership check, and should not pass `alfaclub:<roomId>` unless the Telegram sender is authorized for that room.

title: Workflow input command injection can expose ACP secrets
description: The workflow accepts free-form `slot` and `dry_run` inputs and writes them to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT` without validating them to fixed values first. The subsequent `Run ACP daily market-news runner` step injects `${{ steps.resolve.outputs.slot }}` and `${{ steps.resolve.outputs.dry }}` directly into a bash script while `ACP_ACCESS_TOKEN`, `ACP_REFRESH_TOKEN`, `ACP_OWNER_WALLET`, and `ACP_CLIENT_AGENT_ID` are present in the environment. GitHub expression substitution happens before bash parses the script, so an output value containing shell syntax such as command substitution can be executed in the second step. The runner's own `--slot` validation happens only after the shell has already expanded the injected expression, so it does not prevent the secret-bearing command execution. The fix is to avoid placing untrusted contexts or step outputs directly inside `run:` shell code; use typed `choice`/boolean inputs, validate to `morning` or `checkpoint` before writing outputs, and pass values through environment variables or action arguments without re-parsing them as shell source.

title: Untrusted users can opt into room-default trading identity
description: The commit adds /strategy optin as a non-operator-only command, while only /strategy bias is treated as operator-only. During opt-in, the code resolves the caller's Arena identity and only rejects the env_default fallback. However, resolveArenaIdentityForContext intentionally falls back to a room_default mapping when no per-user mapping exists. Therefore, any non-operator room member can run /strategy optin whenever a room default Arena identity is configured. The counter-trade runner later resolves the same room_default identity for that user and passes its agentId/agentWalletAddress to runArenaTrade, so the user's opt-in can cause trades to be opened using the shared room-default Arena wallet rather than a wallet personally controlled by the user. If multiple users opt in against the same room-default identity, the same upstream fills can also be processed under different senderAddress ledger keys, multiplying executions.

title: Submodule retargets executable skill to personal fork
description: The patch retargets the dgclaw-skill submodule URL from the trusted upstream organization to https://github.com/wenakita/dgclaw-skill.git and pins the submodule to a new fork commit. The repository's arena runtime treats dgclaw-skill as executable operational code: it resolves dgclaw.sh/scripts from the dgclaw checkout and runs them through execFile. The child process is launched with the parent process environment merged in, which can include DGCLAW_API_KEY, ACP_ACCESS_TOKEN, ACP_REFRESH_TOKEN, wallet/session material, and other production secrets. Therefore, if the forked submodule commit contains malicious install/runtime code, the application would execute it in a privileged backend context. This is a supply-chain trust downgrade introduced by the commit.

title: Hermit image pulls mutable third-party code at build time
description: The Hermit Docker image now fetches runtime code directly from external mutable sources: `@virtuals-protocol/acp-cli` is installed without a version or lockfile, and `dgclaw-skill` is cloned from the default `main` branch and installed with normal npm lifecycle scripts enabled. Because this is in the production runner stage, any compromise or malicious update of the npm package, GitHub repository, or selected branch can execute arbitrary code during image build and can also leave malicious code in `/app/dgclaw-skill`. The existing arena runtime executes `dgclaw.sh`, `scripts/deposit.ts`, `scripts/trade.ts`, and `acp` from that workspace while inheriting the service environment. Those environment variables can include ACP tokens, session secrets, database credentials, and signing or trading-related configuration. This makes the image non-reproducible and creates a supply-chain path to secret exfiltration and unauthorized arena actions.

title: Shared impairment escrow can be reassigned and drained
description: The commit adds CreatorOImpairmentClaims and CreatorORecoveryEscrow. Both contracts authorize exactly one `vault` address via a mutable `setVault()` function, while the deployment script describes the contracts as shared and the frontend/server config exposes a single global impairment claims/escrow address to be wired into deployed vaults. If the same auxiliary contracts are reused for multiple vaults, setting `vault` for a new vault revokes the previous vault's ability to mint claims or execute recovery claims. More importantly, CreatorORecoveryEscrow.claimRecovery only checks `msg.sender == vault` and then transfers the requested `amount`; it does not key balances by vault and does not enforce `claimed <= recovered`. Therefore, the currently authorized vault can transfer any token balance held by the shared escrow for any epoch/asset, including recoveries that belonged to earlier vaults. A malicious or later-authorized vault could create its own impairment accounting and call through to the escrow to drain previously escrowed recovery assets.

title: Paymaster swap path bypasses allowlist and swap checks
description: The paymaster validator previously enforced the creator allowlist for validated calls other than setup/relay owner-install flows. This commit adds `validated.mode !== 'swap'` to that exemption, so any call classified as `swap` skips `assertCreatorAllowlisted`. At the same time, the swap classifier allows Universal Router Permit2 opcodes (`PERMIT2_TRANSFER_FROM`, `PERMIT2_PERMIT_BATCH`, `PERMIT2_PERMIT`) and only checks that every opcode is in the allowed set and that some input bytes contain an allowed token address. It never requires at least one actual swap opcode. A caller can therefore craft a Universal Router payload containing only Permit2 commands, embed the USDC address to satisfy the token-reference scan, have it classified as `mode = 'swap'`, and bypass the allowlist. This turns the paymaster endpoint into a sponsor for unauthorized non-swap router operations and can be used to drain or exhaust the paymaster budget via authenticated/sybil smart-wallet senders.

title: Unvalidated Permit2 CSW signatures can drain wallet tokens
description: Before this change, canonical smart-wallet swaps disabled Permit2. The commit explicitly re-enables Permit2 when the execution address is the canonical CSW and adds a CSW signing path that wraps an owner raw ECDSA signature for ERC-1271. That new path only checks that the quote-provided message contains syntactically valid token and spender addresses, then hashes and signs the supplied typed data. It does not require the domain to be the Base Permit2 contract, the spender to be an allowlisted Uniswap router, the token to match the user's input token, the amount to be bounded by the swap amount, or the deadline/chain ID to be sane. Because the signature is valid for the CSW's ERC-1271 `isValidSignature`, a malicious quote payload could request a Permit2 allowance for a valuable CSW token to an attacker spender; once the user signs, the attacker can submit the permit and transfer funds through Permit2. Fix by passing the expected swap context into the signing helper and rejecting any Permit2 payload whose domain, chainId, verifyingContract, primaryType, token, spender, amount, nonce/deadline semantics, and owner/execution wallet do not exactly match an allowlisted swap permit.

title: New room polling can replay stale AlfaClub commands
description: The new polling logic unions the primary AlfaClub room with all configured Hermit command rooms and then runs the normal command executor for each room. In cron mode, `seedHistoryOnlyOnFirstTick` is forced to `false`, so execution is driven by rows that were newly inserted into `alfaclub.chat_ingest`. For a newly enabled room such as 1659, the ingest table has no prior rows, so every slash-command candidate returned by the history page is a brand-new insert even if it was sent long before the bridge started polling that room. Those historical messages are then passed to `executeCommandBatch`. In long-running mode there is a related issue: `bridgeState.seeded` is global rather than per-room, so the first room consumes the one-time seeding guard and later rooms in the same first tick skip the recent-only bootstrap path and execute all unseen history. Because `/alfa` commands are accepted by the bridge and can submit UserOperations such as `buy-key`, this can replay stale chat commands and perform duplicate/unauthorized onchain actions or other side effects without fresh user intent.

title: Waitlist collision adoption can rebind victim accounts
description: The waitlist bootstrap path derives `privyEmail` from Privy's verified email, but falls back to the request body email when Privy server hydration has not exposed a verified email. That request body value is attacker-controlled for direct API callers. The commit now wraps `upsertAccount` in `runWithWaitlistEmailCollisionAdoption` and changes `rebindEmailCollisionProfile` to also accept a profile whose `privy_user_id` already equals the requesting Privy user. When an email collision is raised, the adoption helper can proceed through the bootstrap-email-hint path and `rebindEmailCollisionProfile` updates the `accounts` row to the requester and marks the email verified. This turns profile/account skew or stale partial waitlist state into a full account rebind without requiring the server to prove that the authenticated Privy user owns the email. The rebind should only be allowed when `extractPrivyVerifiedEmail(privyUser)` matches the collision email, or when there is a stronger ownership proof; client-supplied email hints should not authorize persistent identity rebinding.

title: Client email hint can verify or steal waitlist accounts
description: After validating only the Privy token, the handler stores the request body's email as bootstrapEmailHint and sets privyEmail to either Privy's verified email or that untrusted hint. If Privy has no verified email, the attacker-controlled body email is treated as canonical and persisted with emailVerified: true. For existing emails bound to another Privy user, runWithWaitlistEmailCollisionAdoption now passes the same hint into adoptWaitlistBootstrapEmailHintRebind, which only checks that the hint matches the collision email before calling rebindEmailCollisionProfile. This reassigns matching profiles/accounts to the attacker's Privy user without requiring the attacker to control the target email or a target wallet. Before this commit, bootstrap only used extractPrivyVerifiedEmail(context.privyUser), so pre-auth form input could not become a verified canonical account email.

title: CRON_SECRET can now overwrite AlfaClub auth tokens
description: Before this change, POST /api/v1/alfaclub/chat-token required an authenticated admin session. The new cronBootstrap path treats the global CRON_SECRET as sufficient authorization for token writes. That same CRON_SECRET is already used for cron/monitoring surfaces, including the GitHub Actions auth-health monitor, so a principal or environment that only needed read/cron-trigger access is now able to perform a sensitive credential-rotation operation. With the secret, an attacker can submit an arbitrary JWT-shaped value and optionally arbitrary Privy access/refresh tokens. Because only syntactic JWT shape is checked, a fake far-future JWT can pin the DB-backed token source and break bridge auth until an admin repairs it; a valid attacker-controlled AlfaClub triplet could also make the bridge operate under the wrong AlfaClub session.

title: Safe wire script trusts RPC for privileged helper addresses
description: The new `wire-phase3-helper-safe.ts` script is intended to update only the Phase 3 helper, but it calls `wireDeploymentHelpers`, which rewrites all helper slots. The script obtains `phase2Module`, `uniV4Helper`, and `utilsHelper` from live `readContract` calls and immediately signs/executes a Safe transaction with those values. If the RPC endpoint is compromised, malicious, or spoofed during the operation, it can return attacker-controlled module addresses. The Safe owner would then sign a mainnet transaction that wires those malicious addresses while the script only verifies that `phase3Helper` matches the requested value. This is especially dangerous because `phase2Module` is later used via `delegatecall`, giving malicious module code execution in the `DeploymentBatcher` storage/context during user deployment flows.

title: Unvalidated Zora permits can authorize arbitrary CSW spenders
description: The new CSW Permit2 path builds an EIP-712 PermitSingle digest directly from the externally supplied Zora permit and signs it via raw secp256k1/eth_sign, then wraps it as a Coinbase Smart Wallet owner signature. There is no allowlist check that permit.spender is the expected Zora Universal Router, no check that permit.details.token matches the user-selected sell token, no cap that permit.details.amount matches the intended swap amount, and the resulting executable call target is also accepted from the quote response. A malicious or compromised Zora quote API response can therefore ask the user to sign a Permit2 authorization for an attacker-controlled spender and excessive amount. Because this commit makes the CSW raw signature valid for on-chain ERC-1271 verification, the attacker-controlled service that receives the signature can use Permit2 to transfer the CSW's approved token balance. This is especially risky because the raw digest signing path is less user-readable than typed-data signing.

title: Unpaid Stripe bundle row grants deploy entitlements
description: The commit introduces vault_full_deploy as the public purchase SKU and expands any stored vault_full_deploy feature key into Charm, Ajna, Solana mesh, and Meteora entitlements. However, the deploy gating paths that consume this expansion only check status IN ('pending', 'active') and do not require payment_verified_at IS NOT NULL. The Stripe checkout path inserts a pending creator_strategy_features row immediately after creating a Checkout Session, before the user has paid. An authenticated user can therefore start a Stripe checkout for vault_full_deploy, abandon payment, then have resolveCreatorStrategyPlan/listActiveCreatorFeatureKeys expand the unpaid pending row into full Phase 3 entitlements. This can allow unauthorized strategy deployment and paymaster-sponsored UserOps without paying the $499 deploy package. The safer hasLiveActivationForFeature helper already requires payment_verified_at, but these new bundle-aware gating paths do not use the same payment verification requirement.

title: GS026 fallback can sign unverified Safe service transactions
description: The commit adds a fallback for Safe GS026 failures that fetches a transaction by safeTxHash, and if service execution fails with GS026, creates a fresh Safe transaction using only the fetched to/value/data/operation/nonce fields. Because the fallback does not check the tx-service response's Safe address or recompute and compare the Safe transaction hash against the user-supplied safeTxHash, the Safe hash no longer reliably binds what will be signed for the configured protocol Safe. A malicious or wrong Safe transaction returned by the external Safe service, or a hash for a transaction proposed against another Safe, can fail the first execution with GS026 and then be re-signed/executed by the local Safe owner key against the configured Safe. This is especially dangerous for the documented 1-of-N Safe execution flow, where the local owner signature may be sufficient to execute privileged treasury or deployment-batcher calls.

title: Batcher finalize can hijack creator registry entries
description: The commit adds registry auto-wiring during finalizePhase2 for the new Solana ShareOFT bridge. That code calls registerCreatorCoin and setVault/setCreatorWrapper/setCreatorShareOFT/setCreatorGaugeController/setCreatorOracle using only the user-supplied Phase2FinalizeParams. There is no check that an already-registered token's info.creator matches params.owner, no check that existing nonzero fields match the deployment, and no onchain proof that params.owner is the canonical creator/issuer of params.creatorToken. Since DeploymentBatcher finalization is externally callable and _requireOwner only checks msg.sender == params.owner, any user who can get through the deposit path for a token can use the authorized batcher to claim an unregistered token or fill empty fields on a partially registered token. Once the batcher is authorized as a CreatorRegistry factory, the registry accepts these writes. This can squat or hijack registry mappings for a real creator coin, causing protocol/UI/bridge/lottery lookups to resolve to attacker-controlled vault, wrapper, ShareOFT, gauge, oracle, and Solana peer wiring until manually corrected by registry governance.

title: Seed script preserves known placeholder API key
description: The added seed-solana-orchestrator-env.sh reads SOLANA_ORCHESTRATOR_API_KEY from the destination file and reuses it whenever it is non-empty. It does not reject the example value `replace-with-long-random-secret`. If an operator first created `/etc/4626/solana-keeper-orchestrator.env` from the example/template and then runs the newly recommended seed script, the placeholder key is preserved and written back while `SOLANA_ORCHESTRATOR_EXECUTE=1` is enabled. The orchestrator's POST /reconcile endpoint authenticates solely by comparing the bearer token with this environment variable, so anyone who can reach the exposed orchestrator can use the known placeholder token to trigger the predefined keeper actions. Those actions are constrained by onchain/preflight checks, but this is still an authentication bypass for an operational write surface and can cause unauthorized keeper execution, transaction costs, premature Solana fee/winner/graduation operations where configured, or service disruption.

title: Direct public CDP paymaster URL bypasses proxy policy
description: The commit adds a client-side prepared-calls path for adding the Privy embedded EOA as a Coinbase Smart Wallet owner. To sponsor that transaction, the client now reads VITE_CDP_SENDCALLS_PAYMASTER_URL, requires it to be a direct HTTP(S) CDP RPC URL, and forwards it as capabilities.paymasterService.url to wallet_prepareCalls. Because VITE_ variables are compiled into browser-delivered JavaScript and the URL is also handed to the wallet provider, any site visitor can recover the CDP paymaster endpoint and reuse it outside this UI. That bypasses the existing same-origin /api/paymaster proxy model where the backend can authenticate requests and enforce calldata/method allowlists. An attacker can use the exposed endpoint to request sponsorship for arbitrary supported UserOperations, subject only to CDP-side policy, potentially draining the operator's paymaster budget and disrupting sponsored protocol flows.

title: Telegram relay commands execute as relay wallet
description: The new relay formatting and extraction logic deliberately turns Telegram messages such as `/alfa buy-key ...` or legacy `@user: /alfa ...` into executable AlfaClub bridge commands. However, the collected command keeps `sender: entry.sender`, which is the AlfaClub account that posted the relay message, not the Telegram user. `executeCommandBatch` then passes that sender as `senderWallet` and `userId` to the deterministic command executor. The AlfaClub command family includes write-capable subcommands such as `/alfa buy-key`, which resolves the execution context for `params.senderWallet` and submits UserOperations. Therefore, if the relay/bot AlfaClub sender is a hex address with an execution-ready context, any user able to post into the configured Telegram source chat/topic can make the server submit onchain actions as that relay account. The relay should either preserve and verify the real Telegram user's linked wallet identity before executing, or restrict Telegram-relayed commands to read-only subcommands.

title: Telegram webhook accepts lower-privilege link API secret
description: The Telegram webhook is the authenticity boundary for Telegram-originated commands. In this commit, getTelegramWebhookConfig() now derives webhookSecret from TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, then TELEGRAM_BOT_CONFIG_SECRET, then TELEGRAM_LINK_API_SECRET. TELEGRAM_LINK_API_SECRET is documented as a shared secret for server-to-server Telegram endpoints such as unlink, portfolio, and bot-config, not as the Telegram Bot API webhook secret. The webhook handler then accepts any POST whose X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token equals this derived value and trusts the request body as a Telegram update. If a deployment has not explicitly set TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET but has configured TELEGRAM_LINK_API_SECRET, any service or attacker that obtains that lower-privilege secret can POST arbitrary webhook payloads, choose allowed chatId/userId values, and trigger command processing, deterministic keeper commands, trades, or Privy smart-wallet user operations as if Telegram had sent the update. The webhook should require the dedicated TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET for Telegram update authentication, or require an explicit opt-in to reuse another secret after confirming the same value was registered with Telegram.

title: KPR rename makes keeper zone guards fail open on legacy envs
description: The commit changes trust-zone secret and kill-switch lookups to KPR_* only. In the /api/keepr/actions/execute handler, per-zone authentication is only enforced when the new KPR_ZONE_KEY_* value is present. If an operator has migrated the main API key to KPR_API_KEY but still has the previous KEEPR_ZONE_KEY_* variables configured, the new code sees no zone secret and skips the second factor entirely. Separately, isKeeprTrustZoneWriteEnabled returns true when the new KPR_ZONE_DISABLE_* variable is absent, so existing KEEPR_ZONE_DISABLE_* emergency stops are ignored. This is a fail-open migration for controls protecting financial_execution and other keeper trust zones; a caller with the general keeper API key can directly execute supported actions without the intended zone secret, and emergency disable flags may not stop writes.

title: Unrestricted manual deploy can bypass review
description: The workflow correctly restricts automatic push deploys to main, but the manual workflow_dispatch trigger has no equivalent ref guard. For workflow_dispatch, GitHub lets an authorized user select a branch/ref to run the workflow from. Because the job checks out the selected ref and then runs wrangler deploy with CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN and CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID, a user with repository workflow-dispatch access can deploy code from an unreviewed branch to the production Cloudflare Worker. This bypasses branch protection/code review expectations for production deployment and could let malicious Worker code capture proxied Authorization headers, proxy shared secrets, or alter requests/responses. The workflow should either remove workflow_dispatch, add a job-level guard such as `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`, use a protected GitHub environment with required approvals, and ideally pin third-party actions by immutable commit SHA.

title: Role-policy override bypasses vault deployment checks
description: DeploymentBatcher now has a global vaultRolePolicyManager/vaultRolePolicyId configuration and the existing deployPhase2Core path enforces that configured policy. However, the newly added deployPhase2CoreWithRolePolicy function is public and lets the same caller supply any rolePolicyId. Because VaultRolePolicyManager explicitly returns without checks for policyId == 0, a caller can invoke deployPhase2CoreWithRolePolicy(..., 0) to skip the globally configured role policy entirely. The frontend session flow also treats an explicit request rolePolicyId as taking precedence over creator/global defaults and does not reject 0, so the API path can preserve this bypass when a crafted phase2CoreWithRolePolicy call is submitted. This defeats the intended role-policy hardening, such as requireOwnerEoa or allowlisted role requirements.

title: Per-call role policy override bypasses deploy policy
description: The commit adds a global role-policy configuration to DeploymentBatcher, but also exposes deployPhase2CoreWithRolePolicy(params, codeIds, rolePolicyId) to the same public caller set as deployPhase2Core. deployPhase2Core correctly enforces the treasury-configured vaultRolePolicyId. The new variant instead passes the caller-supplied rolePolicyId directly into _enforceRolePolicy. Because VaultRolePolicyManager explicitly returns without checks for policyId == 0, an unallowlisted deployer or a contract owner that should fail requireOwnerEoa can call deployPhase2CoreWithRolePolicy(..., 0) and continue phase 2 while bypassing the configured policy. The frontend session code also allows an explicit request rolePolicyId to override creator/global defaults and does not rewrite or reject 0, so a crafted session payload can preserve the bypassing call. A safe design would make the configured global policy a minimum/mandatory policy, reject 0 when a nonzero global policy is configured, or restrict per-call overrides to protocol-controlled callers and only allow stricter policies.

title: Client-exposed direct CDP paymaster bypasses proxy checks
description: The new prepared-calls helper reads VITE_CDP_SENDCALLS_PAYMASTER_URL directly in frontend code and prefers it over the paymasterUrl argument. It then injects that URL into wallet_prepareCalls capabilities. The account setup flow now requires this direct public URL for sponsored owner approval and passes it into _submitOwnerViaPreparedCallsWithEoaOwner. In a Vite app, VITE_* environment variables are not secrets; they are compiled into browser-delivered JavaScript. As a result, any visitor can recover the direct CDP paymaster RPC URL and use it outside the application. This bypasses the existing server-side /api/paymaster proxy, which keeps CDP_PAYMASTER_URL server-side and enforces authentication, allowed JSON-RPC methods, per-sender/session limits, and strict UserOperation calldata validation before forwarding. An attacker who obtains the direct endpoint can submit their own sponsored UserOperations subject only to external CDP policy, potentially consuming the project's gas sponsorship budget and sponsoring operations the application proxy would reject.

title: Embedded owner install signs unverified prepared userOps
description: For embedded-owner installs, the new preferPreparedReplayableFirst branch executes _submitOwnerViaReplayablePreparedCalls before the self-built relay path. The replayable prepared-calls helper only validates the selector of the locally supplied innerCallData, then asks the wallet provider to prepare a UserOperation, signs the provider-returned signatureRequest.hash, and submits the provider-returned userOp and chainId. It does not decode and compare addOwnerAddress against the intended embedded owner, and it does not locally verify that the returned userOp actually contains the requested sender/callData/chainId. The older self-built relay path did decode addOwnerAddress and reject a mismatch before signing/submission. As a result, if the wallet_prepareCalls response is malicious or corrupted, the app can obtain a valid WebAuthn owner signature over a different replayable owner-management UserOperation and submit it, potentially adding an attacker-controlled owner or otherwise altering the Coinbase Smart Wallet owner state.

title: Paymaster accepts under-validated Swap Proxy calls
description: The paymaster now treats calls to the hard-coded Uniswap Swap Proxy as valid swap calls. Unlike Universal Router calls, these Swap Proxy calls are not ABI-decoded, canonicalized, or checked for allowed router commands, input/output token arguments, recipient, or actual use of the approved/wrapped token. The only payload validation for the new `swap-proxy` path is `assertRawSwapPayloadReferencesToken`, which succeeds if the token address appears anywhere in the calldata. Once this weak check passes, `mode === 'swap'` returns before the stricter second-pass target/selector validation. An authenticated/allowlisted caller can therefore craft arbitrary Swap Proxy calldata that merely embeds the approved token or WETH address and have the paymaster sponsor it, bypassing the intended strict swap policy and potentially draining paymaster gas budget with unauthorized/high-gas operations.

title: Untrusted Zora wallet can become canonical CSW
description: The new single-candidate Zora fallback in wallet synchronization accepts the first EVM address returned by Zora that is not one of the user's non-smart wallets, even when that address was never present as a Privy smart-wallet candidate and is not verified on-chain as controlled by the authenticated user. `syncUserWallets` then treats this address as the persisted canonical smart wallet and writes it into `profiles` and `profile_wallets` with `is_canonical_smart_wallet=true`. Other security checks, notably deploy-session ownership validation, trust this off-chain canonical linkage and allow the recorded active owner wallet to satisfy ownership without an on-chain owner check. Since the threat model treats Zora/external-service data as attacker-controlled, this can let a malicious or poisoned Zora response bind an arbitrary/victim CSW to the attacker's profile and bypass deploy authorization paths that rely on the canonical linkage.

title: Stale CSW recovery can bypass wallet unlinking
description: The wallet sync/delegation changes make the persisted canonical Coinbase Smart Wallet the source of truth even when the current Privy payload does not contain that wallet. This reverses the previous live-wallet invariant and can reassert a smart wallet that the user has unlinked or replaced. The new recovery path also looks up profiles by raw `privyUser.email.address` without requiring Privy's verified-email signal, and by wallet/profile rows without binding the match to the authenticated Privy user id. `resolveCanonicalCsw` then prefers the recovered persisted CSW over the live synced canonical and writes it back to the resolved profile. Downstream deployment authorization relies on these canonical profile-wallet rows, so a stale/recovered canonical can be used to satisfy offchain canonical-wallet linkage checks after unlinking or, in edge cases such as unverified-email/profile-hint collision, pollute another session with a victim CSW.

title: IPFS rewrite exposes untrusted content on trusted 4626.fun origin
description: A new route in `frontend/vercel.json` rewrites `https://4626.fun/ipfs/<cid>` to `https://pinata.4626.fun/ipfs/<cid>` (no 30x status), so browser-visible origin remains `4626.fun`. Since IPFS content is attacker-controllable, this can host arbitrary HTML/JS on a trusted origin. In this codebase, `https://4626.fun` is treated as a trusted origin for authenticated state-changing requests, and auth sessions can be read from shared-domain cookies (`.4626.fun`). This combination means a victim visiting a malicious `4626.fun/ipfs/<cid>` page can execute first-party script that performs authenticated API actions from a trusted origin context (and potentially leak sensitive data accessible to that origin).

title: Unauthenticated VRF request path enables subscription draining
description: This commit adds `ChainlinkVRFAdapter.request()` and `RandomnessRouter.acquireRequest()` as unrestricted external functions. In the intended wiring, the adapter must be granted `authorizedLocalCallers` on `CreatorVRFConsumerV2_5` so it can call `requestRandomWords()`. Because the adapter itself has no caller restriction, any EOA/contract can call it (or call the router, which forwards to it) and trigger privileged VRF requests. That bypasses the original caller-auth model at the edge and enables request spam, LINK subscription depletion, and lottery randomness pipeline DoS/degradation.

title: Allowlist bypass via untrusted creator token parties
description: The commit expands deploy-session allowlist checks to include creator/payoutRecipient/owner addresses resolved from the user-supplied creatorToken. Because creatorToken is provided by the caller and resolveCoinPartiesAndOwner simply reads on-chain contract fields, an attacker can deploy or select a token contract that returns an allowlisted/admin address as creator/payoutRecipient while keeping themselves as owner. assertCreatorTokenAuthority only requires the session to match any party, so the attacker passes authority checks while the allowlist/admin match is satisfied by the forged party address, enabling unauthorized deploy-session creation.

title: Arch B /coin sell uses unvalidated Zora quote calls
description: handleSellViaArchB fetches a trade quote from the Zora API and builds a UserOp call directly from the returned call.target/data while also signing Permit2 payloads from the response. There is no validation or allowlist of the router target or permit contents, and the code explicitly notes the allowlist is not wired. Because the CSW is the sender, a compromised/mitm quote response could craft arbitrary calls or permit approvals and drain user assets.

title: Ajna limit index buffer moves in wrong direction
description: The new Ajna borrow integration computes the `limitIndex` for `drawDebt` by adding `safetySteps` to the oracle‑suggested bucket. However, Ajna bucket indices are inverted relative to price (higher price → lower index, see `tickToAjnaBucket`). Adding steps therefore moves the limit to a *lower* price, loosening the LUP guard instead of tightening it. When withdrawals trigger `_tryAjnaBorrow`, the strategy can open or expand debt even if the Ajna LUP is already below the intended collateral buffer, exposing the USDC collateral to immediate liquidation and potential fund loss for vault shareholders.

title: Sponsored non-owner deposits donate pool assets
description: The commit adds a paymaster management policy and UI for direct inventory deposits. In the paymaster policy, deposit calls are identified by ERC-20 transfer or ERC-1155 safeTransferFrom selectors and are validated without checking that the UserOp sender is the pair owner. The owner check is only applied in the non-deposit branch. The new UI mirrors this by building the deposit plan before enforcing ownerMatches; owner gating only applies to withdraw/configure modes. For Sudoswap pairs, ownership is the liquidity position and withdrawals go to/are controlled by the pair owner; non-owner deposits do not mint LP shares or create a redemption right. As a result, a non-owner can be guided through the official sponsored path to transfer AKITA/FriendKeys into the pool, effectively donating assets to the owner, and the paymaster will subsidize those transfers. This also creates an economic-abuse path against the paymaster by repeatedly submitting dust deposits, subject only to the broader account/rate limits.

title: Cooldown propagation bypass for established ShareOFT holders
description: CreatorOVaultWrapper and AgentOVaultWrapper now return early when the recipient's post-transfer balance is greater than the transfer amount, treating the recipient as an established holder and intentionally not updating lastWrapperDepositBlock[to]. Because the check is based only on whether the recipient had any prior balance, an attacker can prepare a recipient address with a tiny old ShareOFT balance. Later, after wrapping or depositing in the wrapper, the attacker transfers the fresh ShareOFT to that pre-seeded recipient; the recipient's cooldown is not updated, so _requireWrapperCooldown uses the recipient's old/zero cooldown and allows immediate unwrap/withdraw. This weakens the wrapper's flash-loan/MEV protection. The underlying vault-level cooldown may still block some deposit-to-redeem paths when enabled, but the wrapper-level protection is explicitly bypassed and remains relevant for advanced wrap/unwrap flows and any configuration where the vault delay is disabled or shorter than the wrapper policy. The same pattern was added to both creator and agent wrappers.

title: Recent non-stakers can suppress Chip fade attribution
description: For Chip trade-completed cards without a payload userAddress and without an in-batch speaker, the commit adds a lookup into alfaclub.chat_ingest and attributes the card to the newest hex sender in the room within the 2 hour lookback. That query does not verify that the speaker is eligible, staked, human, or otherwise authorized. Once a DB speaker is selected, collectInverseAkitaChatTradeIntents never tries the room creator fallback. The later execution path checks stake eligibility only after the intent has already been attributed; if the selected recent speaker is not eligible, the trade is skipped. In the batch path, the message is also claimed/deduped before execution, so the same Chip card will not be retried with the creator fallback. A room participant can keep a non-staked wallet as the most recent durable speaker before their own or another missing-address Chip OPEN card, causing the intended fade to be suppressed.

title: Forwarded EVM lottery entries are rejected
description: LotteryManager4626.receiveRemoteLotteryEntry now rejects every forwarded payload whose length is not exactly 224 bytes. However the remote EVM ShareOFT implementations still encode only six ABI fields: msgType, buyer, tokenIn, amount, sourceChainId, and buyerCurrentShareBalance, producing a 192-byte payload. On hub delivery, the ShareOFT forwards that unchanged message to LotteryManager4626. The manager emits InvalidPayloadReceived and returns before _handleLotteryEntry, so no lottery entry or VRF request is created. Because the remote submit path deletes the pending entry before _lzSend and the destination handler returns normally on invalid length, the user-paid submission can be consumed without lottery participation. The intended replay hardening should either update all ShareOFT senders to include a unique non-zero sourceEventId or keep backward-compatible handling for non-Solana/EVM lanes until senders are upgraded.

title: Payout recipient invariant fails open on read errors
description: The new catch-all around the CreatorCoin payoutRecipient() read treats every failure as evidence that the asset is not a CreatorCoin. This includes missing-selector errors, but also execution reverts, out-of-gas in a malicious getter, RPC/provider errors, and any other read failure. Because the invariant gate only blocks deployment continuation when violations are recorded, a CreatorCoin or CreatorCoin-like asset whose payoutRecipient read fails can bypass the external earnings lane validation entirely. That can allow post-phase2 deployment stages to proceed even though CreatorCoin external earnings are routed to an unexpected recipient instead of the expected gauge or payout router.

title: AMOE cutover script keeps deprecated publisher key
description: This commit repoints script/execute-v1180-post-broadcast.sh at the live v1.19.1 Registry, DeploymentBatcher, and LotteryManager, but leaves AMOE_PUBLISHER defaulted to 0xAb6d5C10..., which the canonical address documentation explicitly says is no longer the AMOE publisher. The script exports that value into DeployLotteryAmoeRouter and the wiring script. The router constructor uses AMOE_PUBLISHER as the allowlist publisher, and the wiring script also sets both allowlistPublisher and pointsLedgerPublisher to that same value. Those publisher roles can publish one-shot Merkle roots and, for the legacy path, act as the trusted relayer. If operators run the cutover script with defaults, the deprecated personal key retains authority over current lottery entry roots/relay instead of the protocol CSW.

title: Chip trade cards can be mis-attributed to stakers
description: The new Chip handling treats a message as a Chip trade card when either the sender is a known Chip alias or the username is `chip`/`chipbot`, then attributes parsed trade events to `payloadAddress`, otherwise to the most recent hex-address speaker in the provided message batch, and finally to the room creator. The attribution helper does not verify that the recent speaker actually authored the Chip trade, does not require a tight time window, and does not authenticate the Chip message beyond sender/username aliases. Downstream, `executeInverseAkitaChatReaction` performs the stake eligibility check against this attributed address and may submit an inverse Arena/Hyperliquid trade with the shared executor wallet. A non-eligible user who can cause a Chip/trade-completed card without an embedded wallet shortly after an eligible staker speaks can therefore have the bot treat the card as that staker's intent and execute a trade.

title: Client aborts can trip the shared LLM provider circuit
description: The updated LLM retry path now treats an externally aborted AbortSignal as a retryable UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT. generateResponse then catches that error in the generic provider-failure handler, calls markProviderFailure(), and only afterwards notices that the caller's abort signal is set and breaks. Because provider failures open a shared circuit after the configured threshold, an authenticated user can open the streaming agent endpoint, disconnect while the upstream provider request is in flight, and repeat this a few times to mark healthy providers as failed. With the default circuit threshold and per-user/IP stream limits, this can temporarily deny LLM service to other users on the same server process. Previously, request_cancelled was thrown and explicitly rethrown before markProviderFailure(), so client cancellations did not poison provider health.

title: Phase2 provenance bypass enables paymaster gas abuse
description: Before this commit, phase2/phase3 paymaster validation started with vaultValidated=false and required either a matching CREATE2-derived vault address or a matching DeploymentBatcher Phase1Deployed log. The commit changed this to vaultValidated = mode === 'deploy_phase2'. For phase2 calls that do not include a vault codeId, such as finalizePhase2 and aux-only VaultAuxiliaryDeployBatcher flows, canValidateViaCreate2 is false, so the Phase1Deployed check is skipped. The remaining checks only read generic view methods on the supplied vault, wrapper, and shareOFT; these can be satisfied by attacker-controlled contracts returning the expected relationships. Because aux-only calls can set deploy_phase2 mode directly and the auxiliary batcher itself only checks that the supplied vault owner equals params.owner before deploying protocol auxiliaries, an authenticated/allowlisted user can obtain paymaster sponsorship for non-protocol auxiliary deployments or for phase2 operations that would previously have been rejected as not originating from phase1. Onchain DeploymentBatcher phase2/finalize logic still protects real protocol vault state via phase1 state checks, so this is primarily a paymaster fund/gas-abuse issue rather than direct vault asset theft.

title: Self-bundling can spend privileged server keys
description: The commit adds a transport wrapper that intercepts oversized eth_sendUserOperation calls and submits them directly through EntryPoint.handleOps. Because deploy-session UserOps are given 16.75M call gas plus verification gas, they exceed the self-bundle threshold and will use this path. The self-bundle signer is read from DEPLOY_SESSION_SELF_BUNDLE_PRIVATE_KEY, but if that is absent the code silently falls back to KPR_PRIVATE_KEY and then PRIVATE_KEY. Those names are likely to hold privileged keeper/deployer/operator keys elsewhere in the system, not an isolated low-balance bundler key. The selected key is then used to broadcast a 25M-gas transaction without a local handleOps simulation or receipt check before returning success to the deploy workflow. A malicious or compromised authenticated deploy-session user who can create syntactically valid but reverting/racy deployment UserOps can force the backend to burn gas from whichever operational key is configured. This does not expose the private key or make the EOA the smart-wallet caller, but it creates a remote gas-drain/availability risk for keeper/deployer wallets and can strand deploy sessions. The self-bundling path should require a dedicated low-balance key, avoid fallback to generic PRIVATE_KEY/KPR_PRIVATE_KEY, simulate handleOps immediately before broadcast, and fail closed if the dedicated key is not configured.

title: Phase1 sponsorship lacks vaultKind/codeId validation
description: For Phase1 DeploymentBatcher calls, the updated ABI now decodes params containing vaultKind and also accepts legacy overloads. After decoding, validateInnerCalls extracts only creatorToken and owner and then classifies the selector as deploy_phase1. There is no parseOnchainVaultKind check and no comparison of codeIds against resolveDeployLanePhase1CodeIds(vaultKind), unlike the stricter Phase2/auxiliary validation paths. Pass 2 then allows any allowed DeploymentBatcher selector without further argument checks. This means a caller who can reach the paymaster path can submit Phase1 calldata with an invalid vaultKind enum value or invalid/mismatched codeIds. The onchain batcher rejects zero/unapproved Phase1 codeIds and Solidity enum decoding rejects out-of-range vaultKind values, but that rejection occurs during UserOperation execution after sponsorship, potentially charging the paymaster for reverting operations. If the codeIds are approved but cross-lane/mismatched, the paymaster may also subsidize unintended Phase1 deployments rather than the canonical creator/agent lane.

title: Admin deploy sessions bypass fresh Privy reauthentication
description: Deploy-session resume, continue, cancel, and advance paths intentionally set requireFreshPrivyJwt=true because these operations can send deployment UserOperations or mutate deployment state. Before this commit, any cookie or bearer HMAC session also had to present a recently issued Privy JWT linked to the same wallet. The new condition skips that reauthentication whenever the session address is listed in CREATOR_ACCESS_ADMIN_ADDRESSES. However, the HMAC session token format contains only an address and is accepted from either Authorization: Bearer or the cv_auth_session cookie; it does not distinguish a controlled server-admin automation token from an ordinary admin browser session. Therefore, possession of an old/stolen admin session token is now sufficient to continue/cancel/advance admin-owned deploy sessions for up to the session TTL, without the fresh Privy proof that APIAUTH-012 was meant to require. The sessionAddress-to-record ownership check still limits the bypass to deploy sessions whose sessionAddress is the admin address, so this is not a universal unauthenticated bypass, but it weakens a security-critical reauthentication barrier for privileged deploy operations.

title: LLM classifier runs before chat author eligibility check
description: The commit adds an async LLM classification path inside collectInverseAkitaChatTradeIntents. The collection loop only checks that the message has an id/text, is not command-like, and has a hex-looking sender before calling classifyOpinion for top-level loose chatter. The expensive external LLM request is made before resolveInverseAkitaChatAuthorAccess is called, which only happens later inside executeInverseAkitaChatReaction. As a result, any user who can post messages in a configured reaction room with a normal wallet sender can spam arbitrary top-level messages that do not need to match the deterministic trade regex and cause one LLM request per message. Because classification is awaited sequentially per message and defaults to an 8 second timeout, this can exhaust LLM budget/rate limits and create significant latency or availability loss for the bridge before ineligible senders are rejected.

title: AMOE cutover script grants publisher role to deprecated CSW
description: The commit cuts the post-broadcast script over to the v1.19.1 LotteryManager, but the same script still exports AMOE_PUBLISHER as 0xAb6d5..., and then calls the historical v1.16.1 AMOE wiring helper. The router deployment consumes AMOE_PUBLISHER as the constructor allowlistPublisher, and the wiring helper later sets both allowlistPublisher and pointsLedgerPublisher to the same value. This conflicts with the updated v1.19.1 address reference, which states that 0x793c... must be the on-chain allowlist/ledger publisher and that the operator personal CSW 0xAb6d5... is no longer the AMOE publisher. If operators run this cutover path without explicitly overriding AMOE_PUBLISHER, the deprecated personal wallet retains authority to publish one-shot Merkle roots and to submit legacy AMOE entries on the new v1.19.1 router. That can allow lottery entry forgery/misattribution or epoch bricking if that wallet is compromised or no longer controlled under the intended protocol-key policy.

title: Global MCP config exposes 4626 ops tools cross-workspace
description: The commit adds `scripts/apply-operator-cursor-efficiency.sh`, which overwrites `$HOME/.cursor/mcp.json` with Railway and Supabase MCP servers for the 4626 project. Because this is the global Cursor MCP configuration, the authenticated Railway CLI and Supabase MCP project are made available to every Cursor workspace, not just `/workspace/4626`. The docs also instruct operators to run this script as a normal setup step. If the operator later opens an untrusted repository or processes attacker-controlled prompts, that workspace may be able to invoke the globally configured MCP tools and access or mutate 4626 production infrastructure/data, depending on the operator's existing MCP/CLI authentication. This unnecessarily crosses the project trust boundary; sensitive MCP servers should be configured project-locally or gated behind explicit per-use confirmation rather than written globally.

title: Ambiguous oil chat can trigger live trades
description: This commit adds ambiguity handling for concepts such as oil/crude, but `extractChatMarketAsset` returns the first configured candidate when `availableMarkets` is not provided. Most batch/polling paths pass available markets, but the live websocket ingestion path in `chatBridge.ts` calls `collectInverseAkitaChatTradeIntents` without `availableMarkets`. In that path, an ambiguous natural-language message such as “Oil going up finally” is parsed as `xyz:CL` with no `marketClarification`. Since `executeInverseAkitaChatReaction` only skips when `marketClarification` is present, the intent proceeds through normal market validation and can call `runArenaTrade`. This creates a live-path inconsistency where ambiguous chat should ask for clarification but instead can open or close real positions on the shared executor.

title: Activation token bypasses paymaster sponsorship limits
description: The paymaster previously counted final sponsorship methods such as pm_getPaymasterData and eth_sendUserOperation against per-sender and per-session limits. This commit changes the request weight to 0 whenever the activation-owner policy header contains a validly signed activation token. Later validation checks that the activation token claim is active, but it does not consume the claim in the paymaster path. The only new consumption happens in complete-activation after XMTP provisioning. Therefore, until the token expires or the user completes activation, the same token can be reused for repeated sponsored activation owner-install UserOps. Because weight 0 also skips the session limiter, a malicious authenticated user can submit many validly shaped addOwnerAddress(serverOwner) operations with increasing nonces and shift gas costs to the paymaster beyond the intended hourly caps. The remaining IP-level limit reduces throughput but does not enforce the paymaster's financial sponsorship quota.

title: Unbounded waitlist leaderboard cache enables memory DoS
description: The new leaderboard cache stores every distinct key in a module-level Map. The key includes the request page, limit, points type, and optional profile id. The waitlist leaderboard handler clamps limit but does not cap page, and the cache has no max size, LRU eviction, or cleanup of expired entries. Expired entries remain in the Map indefinitely unless the exact key is reused. Because this endpoint is public and the cache key is attacker-controllable via page, an attacker can issue requests such as page=1, page=2, ... to create unbounded cache entries. This can steadily increase memory usage on warm serverless/API instances and cause availability degradation or process restarts. A bounded LRU cache, periodic expired-entry cleanup, page clamping, and/or endpoint rate limiting would mitigate this.

title: Unauthenticated /ready endpoint can block indexer health
description: The new Shovel health sidecar exposes `/ready` on `0.0.0.0` and, for each request, synchronously spawns `psql` to query the production database and then fetches the chain tip from the configured RPC. Because `spawnSync` blocks the Node.js event loop, an unauthenticated remote caller can repeatedly hit `/ready` to tie up the health server, consume DB/RPC resources, and potentially cause `/health` probes to time out or make the indexer service unavailable. The endpoint also returns up to 200 bytes of raw `psql` stderr/stdout in HTTP responses, which may leak internal database host/user/schema details during failures. Readiness checks should be private/authenticated, cached/rate-limited, non-blocking, and should not return raw backend errors.

title: Lottery cutover can strand jackpot payouts
description: The cutover script updates the registry to the new LotteryManager and the frontend defaults also point to that new address. CreatorShareOFT resolves the LotteryManager dynamically from the registry when creating lottery entries, so existing ShareOFT buys will now send entries to the new manager. However, jackpot funds are held by each GaugeController, and GaugeController.payJackpot only accepts calls from its own stored lotteryManager. The script does not iterate registered gauges and call setLotteryManager(newManager), and new deployments through the unchanged DeploymentBatcher are also wired from the batcher's immutable lotteryManager value. As a result, a winning request processed by the new manager can call payJackpot on a gauge still configured for the old manager; that call reverts, is caught by LotteryManager, and the lottery result is still consumed with a zero payout. This is an economic-integrity/availability issue for lottery rewards rather than direct fund theft.

title: Canary verifier ignores unsafe jackpot and VRF state
description: The added `verify-lottery-canary-phase0.ts` script treats `singleVaultJackpotOnly()` and `deferredVrfQueueLength()` as passing if the calls merely succeed. It does not require `singleVaultJackpotOnly === true` or `deferredVrfQueueLength === 0`, even though the checklist requires those exact states before canary traffic. As a result, any post-remediation LotteryManager where an owner has flipped multi-vault jackpots on, or where deferred VRF results are still pending, can still produce `readyForBaseOddsCanary: true` and no blocker. If operators or automation rely on that verdict to enable traffic, the lottery could run with the R-H05 single-vault payout mitigation disabled or with unresolved VRF backlog, allowing mis-scoped jackpot payouts or settlement issues.

title: Webhook raw-body hardening is bypassed by Vercel catch-all
description: The new Stripe and X webhook handlers require exact raw bytes and reject any non-null parsed object body. Dedicated wrapper files were added with bodyParser:false, but frontend/vercel.json routes all /api/* requests to /api/[...path] before the filesystem route is evaluated, and no explicit Vercel route was added for /api/x/account-activity/webhook or /api/creator/strategy/stripe/webhook. Because those paths are still present in the catch-all route map, production requests can be dispatched by the catch-all function with Vercel's default body parsing enabled. For application/json webhooks, req.body will be an object, causing X webhooks to return invalid_webhook_body and Stripe webhooks to return raw_body_unavailable. This breaks X engagement processing and, more importantly, Stripe checkout activation finalization after payment.

title: Agent ShareOFT skips cooldown propagation via DEX addresses
description: AgentOVaultWrapper relies on lastWrapperDepositBlock being propagated across ShareOFT transfers so a user cannot deposit or wrap, move the newly minted ShareOFT to a fresh address, and immediately withdraw or unwrap from that fresh address. The new AgentShareOFT._update logic returns before calling propagateCooldownOnTransfer whenever the sender or recipient is classified as SwapOnly or NoFees. Because SwapOnly addresses are public trading venues, a cooled-down sender can route ShareOFT through such a venue to a new address without copying lastWrapperDepositBlock. That recipient then has no wrapper cooldown recorded, while AgentOVaultWrapper only checks the caller's own lastWrapperDepositBlock. This weakens the same-block/flash-loan withdrawal protection for the Agent lane and is inconsistent with the stated hook invariant that all non-mint/non-burn ERC20 movements should propagate cooldown state.

title: Public stats leaks recent waitlist member identities
description: The `/api/waitlist/stats` handler is public and does not require a session. This commit changed the avatar source from only the public leaderboard slice to `fetchSocialProofAvatars`, which falls back to `fetchRecentMemberAvatars` when there are fewer than 12 top-point avatars. The new SQL selects the newest verified-email profiles (`p.email IS NOT NULL`, ordered by `p.id DESC`) and returns avatar data plus Zora handle/basename and a link address. As a result, any unauthenticated caller can poll the stats endpoint to learn which Zora handles or wallet addresses recently joined the waitlist, even if those users are not on the public leaderboard. This leaks waitlist membership and signup recency metadata tied to public identities.

title: Cutover script exposes treasury private key in process args
description: The newly added `republish-amoe-roots-treasury-cutover.sh` sources `.env` and then invokes `cast send` repeatedly with `--private-key "$PRIVATE_KEY"`. Command-line arguments are commonly visible through process-list interfaces such as `ps` or `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` to other local users or monitoring/CI tooling. Because this key is described as the treasury owner/router owner key, disclosure could allow an attacker who observes the process arguments to publish AMOE roots or perform other owner-level actions permitted by that key. This is not remotely exploitable by itself, but it is an operational secret exposure in a script intended for production cutover use.

title: Share-mesh LP manager wiring always reverts
description: The commit introduces a DeploymentBatcherShareMeshHelper that deploys/configures the post-CCA LP manager and then calls cca.setLpManager(out.lpManager). However, CCALaunchArm.setLpManager is protected by onlyApprovedOrOwner, and the Phase 2 setup only approves the DeploymentBatcher itself and optionally the VaultActivationBatcher. The actual msg.sender for setLpManager is the ShareMeshHelper contract, not the DeploymentBatcher, and the CCALaunchArm ownership is transferred to protocolTreasury during finalize. Therefore the new canonical deployShareMeshLpManager path reverts at the final wiring step for real CCALaunchArm instances. Because seedLpManager requires lpManager to be set, the ShareOFT LP reserve and swept auction currency retained by the CCA arm cannot be seeded through the intended automation path and remain unavailable unless the protocol treasury performs manual recovery/configuration.

title: Child process stderr is echoed into public chat
description: The new failure-detail helpers collect lines from run.error, run.stderr, and run.stdout, only filtering out a leading "Command failed:" line. Those strings come from dgclaw/ACP/tsx child processes that run with sensitive environment and local ACP state. The selected lines are then appended directly to public chat replies for inverse trade failures and /h arena failures. A room participant can trigger inverse trade attempts, and authorized arena commands also post replies into the room, so any secret-bearing CLI diagnostic, stack trace, config dump, token, private key fragment, or internal path emitted on stdout/stderr can be exposed to other chat participants. The code should either avoid returning raw child-process output to chat or apply strict allowlisted error codes/redaction before replying.

title: Protocol automation Safe is 1-of-1 hot keeper controlled
description: The new deployment path creates the protocol automation Safe with a single owner, the canonical keeper EOA, and a threshold of 1. The same commit then hardcodes that Safe as the default protocolAutomation address used for greenfield strategy deployment/operation. Existing deployment logic gives this protocolAutomation address privileged strategy roles: Charm vault manager and AjnaVaultAuth admin. Ajna admin authority can pause/unpause, change swapper/keeper roles, set deposit/buffer/fee parameters, and set the minimum bucket. As a result, compromise or misuse of the broadly deployed KPR_PRIVATE_KEY now gives unilateral hot-key control over privileged strategy administration that was previously intended to be separated from the cold treasury Safe/multisig lane. This is mostly an operational/key-management exposure rather than a permissionless on-chain exploit, so it is downgraded from high to medium.

title: Wallet edit flow enables waitlist point farming
description: This commit adds an Edit action for linked waitlist wallets that calls unlinkAndSyncPrivyProvider for external_eoa and then reopens the wallet connect step. The server-side scoring model only checks whether the provider is currently linked before awarding points. After unlinking, providerWasAlreadyLinked returns false, and external_eoa point events are keyed as link_external_eoa:<address>.
